Paḷani
------------------------------------------
God सुब्रह्मण्य is one of the most popular deities of हिन्दुइस्म्, especially in Tamil Nadu. Out of the six well-known temples dedicated to him, the one at पऌअनि is perhaps the most famous one.
Situated in the मदुरै district of Tamil Nadu, it lies to the north-west of मदुरै at a distance of 100 kms. (62 miles).
The temple itself has been built on the hill Śivagiri which is 40 metres (450 feet) high with 659 steps leading to it.
As per the sthaḷapurāṇa, or local legends, the sage अगस्त्य requested Lord शिव and पार्वती to establish themselves on the two hills which are now known as Śivagiri and Śaktigiri, which they did. Then अगस्त्य commissioned his giant disciple Iḍumbara to carry the two hills on a kāvaḍi (a wooden stick with two baskets at the ends). On the way to his destination, Iḍumbara rested his kāvaḍi and himself at the place now known as पऌअनि. Meanwhile सुब्रह्मण्य (also known as स्कन्द, गुह and षण्मुख) who had come away after quarreling with his parents शिव and पार्वती, had settled himself on the Śivagiri hill making it impossible for Iḍumbara even to lift his kāvaḍi. Finally at his request Subrah-maṇya made him dvārapālaka (gate keeper) and also approved his request that devotees who bring offerings in a kāvaḍi be specially blessed.
The image is made of navapāṣāṇas (nine kinds of poisons or mineral substances) blended together in certain proportions resulting in a wax-like substance. The sage Bhogar was the one who prepared the icon (There is a shrine dedicated to him also).
Since सुब्रह्मण्य came as a boy-ascetic, the image is very simple, shorn of all dresses and ornaments except for kaupīnam (loin cloth) and a दण्ड (a staff). Hence the deity is also called Bāla- daṇḍāyudhapāṇi (the child holding a staff as a weapon). It faces west.
According to another legend, Ceraman Perumāḷ, the king of Cera dynasty, retrieved the ancient image after a dream revelation and built the present temple.
Though the face of the deity is beautiful, the whole body is rough. Whether it is due to the ravages wrought by time or due to the scrapping of the body-surface by some sages of the siddha tradition (alchemists or doctors using plant products as medicines) because of its curative properties, it is difficult to say.
In fact in A.

, an attempt was made to replace the ‘worn out’ image with a new one but it was stoutly resisted by the devotees.
The image wears a garland and रुद्राक्ष beads (Eleocarpus ganitras).
There are six pūjas or ceremonial worships everyday from morning to night.
As many as ten abhiṣekas (purificatory baths) are done every day with various substances such as gingelly oil, rice powder, turmeric powder, pañcāmṛtam (with five sweet ingredients) and विभूति (ash). After the abhiṣekas the image is decorated in various forms.
The pañcāmṛta is not only very tasty, but can also be preserved for a long time.
The sandal paste smeared on the head of the deity on the previous day is removed only the next morning. It is believed to have miraculous healing powers.
Of the various festivals celebrated at the temple, the Taipūṣam (puṣyapūrṇimā, the full मोओन् day of puṣyamāsa, generally during January-February) is the most important one.
Pilgrims who visit the shrine on this day observe the vow of continence and walk barefooted all the way from their places. They also carry the kāvaḍi in which they may bring a litter of wood or pots of water for अभिषेक. On this occasion, the diamond-encrusted Vel or javelin of the Lord सुब्रह्मण्य of the temple at Karaikudi is also ceremonially brought to this pilgrim centre.
The other festivals of importance are Paṅguni Uttaram in April and स्कन्द Ṣasṭhi in July.
It is interesting to note that Muslims call this deity as Paḷanibābā and come to the temple to offer their prayer at the rear side.
